industry: Cokemaking & Logistics (Domestic Coke, Brazil Coke, Logistics)
drawdown_context: SXC entered the cutoff window as a small-cap cokemaker whose long-term, take-or-pay contract book is rolling at the trough. Cliffs Steel and U.S. Steel together produced 78.6% of FY24 revenue (Cliffs $1,237.0M / 63.9%; U.S. Steel $284.6M / 14.7%); two of five U.S. plants (Granite City, Haverhill II) had contracts expiring June 2025, with Jewell's Cliffs Steel piece following December 2025. The October 2024 Granite City extension to June 30, 2025 was already explicitly disclosed as 'turn-down capacity' at '295 thousand tons' vs prior 650-ton nameplate at 'significantly lower' economics. Q1 2025 results then confirmed the squeeze: revenue fell -10.7% YoY to $436.0M with management citing 'lower volumes and pricing in our Domestic Coke segment as a result of challenging blast furnace coke spot market conditions as well as the impact of the Granite City contract extension economics.' Secular EAF / decarbonization pressure plus an idiosyncratic concentration cliff drove the drawdown.

rfm_tuples.R: [10-K Item 1 plant table:] 'Granite City... U.S. Steel June 2025 Capacity (5)... (5) In October 2024, the Granite City long-term, take-or-pay agreement with U.S. Steel was extended through June 30, 2025, with an option for U.S. Steel to extend for an additional six months. Under the terms of the extension, Granite City will operate at a turn-down capacity, supplying 295 thousand tons of coke to U.S. Steel during the initial six-month term. The terms of the extension includes a turn down fee, but...' [10-K MD&A Recent Developments].
rfm_tuples.f: MODE A: registry/calendar confirmation of contract roll cliff in the contract table; MODE B: claim_evolution test between 10-K (Feb 2025) and Q1 2025 10-Q (Apr 30 2025) -- did the 'option for U.S. Steel to extend for an additional six months' get exercised cleanly, or did the contract get re-extended in a way that signals U.S. Steel cannot find a long-term replacement?
rfm_tuples.M_source: 10-K Item 1 + MD&A + Q1 2025 10-Q (0001514705-25-000007) MD&A Recent Developments
rfm_tuples.M_value: Mode A confirms: 650-thousand-ton plant cut to 295 thousand tons effective Oct 2024 at 'turn-down capacity.' Mode B catches the drift: Q1 2025 10-Q updates the extension WITHOUT activating the original 6-month option -- instead, 'In April 2025, the Granite City long-term, take-or-pay agreement... was extended through September 30, 2025, with an option for U.S. Steel to extend for an additional three months through December 31, 2025. The provisions and economics of this extension remain unchanged.' Three-month rolling extensions at distressed turn-down economics is the signature of a customer who has not solved its captive-coke problem and is keeping SXC alive month-to-month rather than committing to a multi-year deal.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Mode B is the kill shot. The original 10-K language framed the situation as a clean June-2025 expiry with a single 6-month option. The Q1 2025 update shows the option was NOT exercised on its original terms; instead the contract was sliced into smaller 3-month renewals at the same depressed economics. Multi-quarter erosion of contract duration at a long-term-contract company is the framework's strongest distress tell.

rfm_tuples.f: MODE A: customer-concentration arithmetic. Top-2 customers are >78% of revenue; what is the receivables-concentration trend over the 12 months that include the U.S. Steel / Nippon overhang and the Granite City turn-down?
rfm_tuples.M_source: 10-K Note on Significant Customers + balance sheet roll
rfm_tuples.M_value: Top-2 = 78.6% of FY24 revenue (FY23: 80.0%; FY22: 74.4%) -- structurally HIGH. Receivables concentration moved from 50% (FY23) to 59% (FY24) -- i.e., the AR base is rotating MORE toward the two distressed steel counterparties, not less. Mode B: Q1 2025 10-Q updates Cliffs Steel to $299.3M / U.S. Steel $60.0M of $436.0M total revenue (Cliffs 68.6%, U.S. Steel 13.8%, combined 82.4%) -- concentration is ACCELERATING into the trough rather than diversifying.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Two-customer concentration above 80% with the AR mix actively rotating toward those two is the structural reason the framework should be SHORT this name. Even with a 'take-or-pay' contractual wrapper, a customer mix where (i) one is exiting captive coke (U.S. Steel / Granite City) and (ii) the other is the dominant US blast-furnace consolidator under its own decarbonization plan (Cliffs Steel) leaves no demand re-allocation path.

rfm_tuples.R: [Foundry coke expansion language:] 'Our principal cokemaking products and services include: ...continued expansion into the foundry coke market.' [10-K MD&A:] no quantified 2025 foundry coke revenue guide; the spot/export channel is described as the placement vehicle for 'non-contracted blast coke produced utilizing capacity in excess of that reserved for the long-term, take-or-pay agreement.'
rfm_tuples.f: MODE B: 'what should be verifiable that they didn't say?' If the take-or-pay book is rolling at trough, the bridge claim is 'we'll redeploy capacity into foundry / spot / export.' Quantify the size of that bridge.
rfm_tuples.M_value: 10-K names foundry-coke expansion as a forward initiative but provides NO tonnage guide, NO pricing guide, and NO 2025 EBITDA bridge. Q1 2025 10-Q then quantifies the offset that did NOT materialize: 'lower volumes and pricing in our Domestic Coke segment as a result of challenging blast furnace coke spot market conditions.' Spot/export coke is the only candidate replacement for U.S. Steel's 295-650 thousand ton/year placement, and management is explicitly saying the spot market is challenged. Mode B = the bridge claim is unbacked.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: The 10-K leaves the audience to infer that foundry / spot will plug the contract-roll gap, but the Q1 2025 print explicitly says the spot market is the SOURCE of the squeeze, not the solution. Honest disclosure would have either quantified the foundry pivot or removed it from the narrative.

rfm_tuples.R: 'There have been no share repurchases since the first quarter of 2020 as the Company has suspended additional repurchases, leaving $96.3 million available under the authorized repurchase program as of December 31, 2024.' [And dividend per share:] $0.10 raised to $0.12 effective H2 2024 ('quarterly increase of 20 percent'), declared again at $0.12 on January 30, 2025.
rfm_tuples.f: MODE B: capital_allocation_tell. Does the buyback/dividend pattern look like (a) a company preserving optionality through a contract trough, (b) a company defending the print, or (c) a company in genuine cash-conservation mode?
rfm_tuples.M_value: Buyback authorization is 5+ years cold ($96.3M unused since Q1 2020 trough) -- management is NOT defending the price into a roll-cliff (anti-MGPI). Dividend was actually RAISED 20% in H2 2024 ($0.10 -> $0.12) and re-declared at $0.12 in January 2025. The dividend raise INTO a known June 2025 contract cliff is harder to read: in a candor frame it signals Board confidence; in a Mode B frame, it could be Board commitment-device intended to anchor the equity story while contract economics deteriorate.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: The buyback is unambiguously non-defensive, which is honesty-positive. The dividend RAISE into the contract cliff is the soft spot -- it is consistent with either genuine confidence (the take-or-pay re-extension fees being read as durable) or with Board-anchoring behavior. Cannot disambiguate from the filing alone.

BUT: Moody's outlook stepped DOWN from 'positive' to 'stable' in October 2024 -- the exact month the Granite City contract was extended at turn-down economics. Mode B: rating-agency timing aligns with the contract-roll bad news, which means the bond market was reading the same signal in real time even though equity dividend was being raised.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Auditor history is genuinely clean and not a short signal. The Mode B tell is the Moody's outlook downgrade timed precisely to the Granite City extension month -- credit market saw the deterioration, and the rating action is an external corroborator of the contract-cliff thesis. Net: this is one mild yellow within a clean auditor frame.

This is the one clean dimension of the SXC profile -- it argues against framing this as fraud risk; the risk is structural contract-roll, not management-malfeasance.

rfm_tuples.f: MODE A: covenant_status + maturity_wall. Revolver matures 2026 (within 18 months of cutoff); senior notes 2029. Liquidity headroom vs the contract-roll cash-flow risk.
rfm_tuples.M_value: Total debt $500M (one bond, one revolver), all secured. $189.6M cash + $350M undrawn revolver = $539.6M liquidity headroom against $500M debt. No covenant breach disclosed. BUT: revolver matures 2026 and will need to be refinanced inside the contract-trough window -- a renewal in mid-2026 with the contract book half-rolled at the turn-down economics is a non-trivial market-access risk, even if not yet impaired.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Mode A is clean (liquidity > debt, no covenant breach), so this is not a near-term default story. Mode B yellow: the 2026 revolver refi will price off whatever the spot/foundry coke book and the Cliffs/U.S. Steel renewal landscape look like in 2026 -- the same risk the equity is repricing. Not severe enough to short on alone, but it caps the recovery optionality.

rfm_tuples.R: [10-K MD&A Recent Developments + Q1 2025 10-Q MD&A] both quietly omit any discussion of the U.S. Steel / Nippon Steel acquisition situation that is the dominant counter-party governance overhang on Granite City; no reference to 'Nippon,' 'definitive agreement,' or 'strategic alternative' appears anywhere in the 10-K body.
rfm_tuples.f: MODE B: counterparty disclosure mirror -- when one of your two largest customers is the subject of a politically-contested merger that materially affects whether your contract counterparty even exists in 18 months, the absence of any discussion is itself the tell.
rfm_tuples.M_source: 10-K full text + Q1 2025 10-Q full text grep ('Nippon', 'merger', 'strategic alternative', 'definitive agreement')
rfm_tuples.M_value: Zero mentions of the U.S. Steel corporate-control situation in either filing. Standard risk-factor language about 'severe financial hardship or bankruptcy of one or more of our major customers' is present but generic. The specific counterparty-governance overhang that explains why U.S. Steel is granting 3-month rolling contract extensions instead of multi-year renewals is not named.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Mode B catches what Mode A misses. The framework's strongest finding is the gap: management knows the most material reason U.S. Steel cannot commit to a multi-year Granite City renewal (its own corporate-control uncertainty), yet the filings discuss the contract extension purely as a commercial event. Honest disclosure would have named the counterparty-governance risk; omitting it lets the equity holder under-price the duration of the trough.

The Mode B yellow is on long-lived asset impairment testing: a 650-ton-capacity plant whose take-or-pay anchor has been replaced by 3-month rolling 295-ton extensions arguably crosses the 'significant adverse change' triggering threshold. supplemental_signals.control_assertion: SXC is a STRUCTURAL-CONCENTRATION distress case rather than a fraud/lying case. The framework's value-add here is Mode B (counterparty disclosure mirror + claim_evolution + asset-group impairment trigger) catching the contract-cliff economics that Mode A registry checks would miss because each individual filing line is technically truthful. Insider/auditor/covenant signals are clean -- this is not a 'management is lying' story; it is a 'management is structurally trapped' story with material omissions about WHY.

summary: SXC is a SHORT-tier name driven by structural customer-concentration and contract-roll cliff rather than fraud signals. Cliffs Steel (63.9%) + U.S. Steel (14.7%) = 78.6% of FY24 revenue, with Q1 2025 mix accelerating to 82.4% and AR concentration rotating from 50% to 59% in one year -- the customer book is becoming more concentrated into the trough, not less. Two of five U.S. plants (Granite City, Haverhill II) had take-or-pay anchors expiring in June 2025, with Jewell's Cliffs Steel piece following in December 2025. The strongest framework finding is Mode B claim_evolution: the 10-K disclosed the Granite City situation as a single June-2025 expiry with one optional 6-month extension at turn-down (295 of 650 tons) economics. The Q1 2025 10-Q (Apr 30 2025) then updated that to a fresh April extension through September 30, 2025 with only a 3-month follow-on option at 'unchanged' distressed economics -- the contract is being sliced into 3-month rolling renewals because U.S. Steel cannot commit to longer durations during its own corporate-control situation. The 10-K does not name the counterparty governance overhang (Nippon situation), a Mode B counterparty-disclosure omission. Moody's stepped outlook from positive to stable in October 2024 -- the same month the Granite City extension was first executed -- confirming the bond market was reading the same signal even as the Board raised the dividend 20%. Honesty signals are clean (KPMG 10-yr tenure, effective ICFR, no going concern, buyback frozen since 2020 = non-defensive, no opportunistic insider sales, no 10b5-1 amendments) -- this is NOT a 'lying' case in the MGPI sense, it is a structural concentration / contract-roll case where the omissions are about WHY the contracts are rolling at distressed economics rather than that they ARE rolling. The framework should put SXC in the SHORT-tier with composite in the moderate-elevated range (~0.55-0.65) -- not the 0.85+ tier reserved for active concealment, but well above the 0.40 neutral line.
